title: Best Phoenix Dehumidifier (2026): 200 MAX, DryMAX & More
h1: The Best Phoenix Dehumidifiers for Restoration and Drying
dek: Phoenix builds LGR workhorses for the crews who dry out flooded buildings. Here's how the lineup sorts out — and when a homeowner should own one.
description: The best Phoenix dehumidifier for your job: the 200 MAX, 250 MAX, DryMAX and DryMAX XL LGRs plus the D385 desiccant, compared by size and use.
intro: A **Phoenix dehumidifier** is the kind of machine you see stacked in a restoration van or humming in a gutted basement after a pipe bursts. Phoenix is the professional drying brand of Therma-Stor, the Madison, Wisconsin, company that also makes Santa Fe and Ultra-Aire home dehumidifiers, and its LGR units are built for one job: pulling a soaked structure back to normal moisture levels as fast as possible.

That focus shapes everything about them. Phoenix machines carry built-in condensate pumps, rugged housings and wheels, and they're rated at the warm, wet test conditions restoration pros use rather than the cooler test applied to household units. They also cost several times what a good 50-pint home dehumidifier does, so the first question is whether you need one at all.

Below, we sort the current Phoenix lineup by the job each model suits, explain the older R-series names you'll still find on used listings, and point homeowners toward cheaper routes where they make more sense.
topPicksLead: For most restoration buyers, the **Phoenix 200 MAX** is the Phoenix to own: a full-size LGR that handles typical water-damage jobs without the bulk of the biggest units.

products.name: Phoenix 200 MAX LGR Dehumidifier
pros: Full-size LGR capacity for everyday water-damage jobs
Rugged housing with wheels and handle
cons: Heavy to carry up and down stairs
products.whyWeLoveIt: The 200 MAX is the middle of the Phoenix range in the best sense: big enough to dry a flooded basement or several rooms, small enough that one tech can roll it in. It's the model most restoration shoppers search for by name, and for good reason.
products.performance: Like every Phoenix LGR, it pre-cools incoming air so it keeps condensing water as the space gets drier, which is what separates a restoration dehumidifier from a household box. Phoenix publishes both AHAM and saturation ratings on its spec sheet; compare the AHAM figure against other brands, not the larger saturation number. Owners in the trade describe it as a dependable fleet machine, with the condensate pump as the part most likely to need service over years of use.

products.name: Phoenix DryMAX LGR Dehumidifier
pros: Compact body is easy to move and stack in a van
LGR drying in a smaller package
Bluetooth (BLE) version available for job monitoring
cons: Less capacity than the full-size MAX units
Still far pricier than a home dehumidifier
products.whyWeLoveIt: Not every loss is a flooded basement. The DryMAX brings LGR performance to bathrooms, kitchens, closets and single rooms, and its smaller size makes it the easiest Phoenix to carry up a staircase.
products.performance: It's the go-to when you need several machines spread across a house rather than one big one in the middle. The DryMAX BLE adds Bluetooth so a tech can check readings from a phone instead of opening up the machine. If you're a homeowner with a chronically wet crawl space, though, a dedicated crawl-space unit is cheaper and better suited to running year-round.

products.name: Phoenix DryMAX XL LGR Dehumidifier
pros: More capacity than the standard DryMAX
cons: Larger and heavier than the DryMAX
Not a match for the 250 MAX on big losses
products.whyWeLoveIt: The XL is for crews who like the DryMAX's portability but keep wishing it pulled a bit more water. It sits between the compact DryMAX and the full-size MAX machines.
products.performance: It suits mid-size losses — a finished basement room, a kitchen and adjoining hallway — where a full-size unit would be awkward to place. As with any Phoenix, check the current spec sheet for exact AHAM pints, amp draw and weight before you buy, since the brand has revised models over the years.

products.name: Phoenix 250 MAX LGR Dehumidifier
pros: The highest-capacity LGR in this lineup
Fewer machines needed on big jobs
cons: Big, heavy and harder to place
More amp draw to plan around
products.whyWeLoveIt: When a whole floor or a commercial space is wet, one big machine is often easier to manage than three small ones. The 250 MAX is Phoenix's answer for large, open losses.
products.performance: It's built for jobs where water volume, not floor plan, is the limiting factor: open basements, commercial suites, new construction. Plan the electrical side first; large LGRs draw enough current that you can't stack several on one household circuit along with air movers. The older R250 is its predecessor, and you'll still find plenty on the used market.

products.name: Phoenix D385 Desiccant Dehumidifier
pros: Keeps drying in cold spaces where compressors slow down
Reaches very low humidity for dense materials
cons: Needs exhaust ducting for the wet air
Uses more energy than an LGR in warm conditions
products.whyWeLoveIt: Hardwood, plaster and concrete hold water stubbornly, and a cold building slows any compressor. A desiccant rotor doesn't care about temperature the same way, which makes the D385 the specialist tool in the Phoenix range.
products.performance: Instead of condensing water, it adsorbs moisture onto a rotating desiccant wheel and blows the damp exhaust outside through a duct. Restoration pros use desiccants for winter jobs, unheated buildings and stubborn materials. For homeowners, a small residential desiccant unit is a far better fit; see our [best desiccant dehumidifier](/best/best-desiccant-dehumidifier/) guide.

products.name: AlorAir Storm LGR Extreme Dehumidifier
pros: Real LGR drying for a fraction of the cost
cons: Smaller dealer and service network than Phoenix
Less common in rental and restoration fleets
products.whyWeLoveIt: If you're a homeowner or a small contractor who wants restoration-style drying without a restoration-fleet price, this is the machine we'd look at first.
products.performance: AlorAir rates it at 85 pints a day at AHAM conditions and 180 at saturation, covering up to about 2,300 square feet, with a pump that lifts water 14.7 feet. That's in the same working class as compact pro LGRs. Compare it with the rest of the field in our [best commercial dehumidifier](/best/best-commercial-dehumidifier/) roundup.

items.label: AHAM test conditions — the fairest number for comparing restoration units
Saturation conditions, which produce the biggest number on the box
Typical household circuit, which limits how many LGRs you can run at once

blocks.text: Restoration brands list two capacities because pros use both: AHAM for comparing machines, saturation for estimating a freshly flooded space. Home dehumidifiers are rated under a cooler DOE test, so a Phoenix number and a household number aren't measured the same way.

We don't run a lab or a restoration crew. We sorted the Phoenix lineup using the manufacturer's published specifications and manuals, restoration-supplier listings, the CPSC recall database and what owners in the trade report after seasons of use.

We weighted the factors that matter on a job: AHAM capacity for the size of loss, portability (stairs and vans are real constraints), amp draw, self-draining and parts support. We also included one cheaper LGR, because many people searching for Phoenix are homeowners who don't need a fleet machine.

sections.heading: What to look for in a Phoenix dehumidifier

items.label: AHAM pints, not saturation pints
items.text: Compare models on the AHAM figure. The saturation number is real but describes a much wetter room than most jobs.

items.label: Size for the loss, not the house
items.text: A single room or bathroom suits a DryMAX; a flooded basement suits a 200 MAX; open commercial losses call for a 250 MAX or several machines.

items.label: Amp draw and circuits
items.text: Add up the amps of every dehumidifier and air mover on a circuit. Tripped breakers overnight cost drying time.

items.label: LGR or desiccant
items.text: LGR for most jobs; desiccant for cold buildings or dense materials that need very dry air.

items.label: Parts and manuals
items.text: Note the model and serial number before you buy used, so you can get the right manual and parts list.
sub: Check the pump, float switch and hoses on any used unit.
Ask whether filters and coils have been cleaned.

blocks.text: What about the Phoenix 200 HT and the R-series?

The **HT** designation marks a high-temperature version of the 200 intended for hot drying conditions, such as jobs that pair dehumidifiers with heat. The **R200** and **R250** are earlier-generation LGRs that the MAX models succeeded. Both still turn up on used listings and in rental fleets; they can be good buys if the pump and coil have been maintained, but get the serial number so you can confirm parts availability first.

sections.heading: Phoenix manuals, parts lists and repairs

blocks.text: Phoenix posts owner's manuals and technical literature on its website, organized by model. The model and serial number on the unit's data plate tell you which revision you have, which matters because parts can change between production runs. If you're looking for a DryMAX LGR manual or parts list for an older unit, contact a Phoenix distributor with that serial number.

items: **Air filter:** the cheapest maintenance item and the one most often neglected. A clogged filter cuts capacity and stresses the compressor.
**Condensate pump and float:** the most common service part on any restoration LGR. If the unit shuts off with a full reservoir, start here.
**Hoses:** kinks and cracks cause many "pump failures." Keep spares on the truck.
**Coil cleaning:** jobs are dusty. A dirty coil quietly reduces water removal.

blocks.title: Before you call for service
blocks.text: Check the breaker, filter and drain hose first. Many no-water or shut-off complaints trace back to one of the three. Our [dehumidifier not collecting water](/guides/dehumidifier-not-collecting-water/) guide covers the basics.

sections.heading: Should a homeowner buy a Phoenix?

blocks.text: Usually not for a one-time flood. Renting a restoration LGR for a few days typically costs far less than buying, and your insurer may cover professional mitigation anyway. Our [dehumidifier rental guide](/guides/dehumidifier-rental/) walks through how that works, and our [water damage dehumidifier](/best/best-dehumidifier-for-water-damage/) guide covers the first 48 hours.

Buying makes sense if you own rental properties, live where frozen pipes are a yearly risk, or run a trade business. For routine dampness, a household unit or an encapsulated [crawl space dehumidifier](/best/best-crawl-space-dehumidifier/) is quieter, cheaper to run and designed to work year-round. If you like Therma-Stor's engineering for home use, its [Santa Fe line](/best/best-santa-fe-dehumidifier/) is the residential sibling.

For restoration work, the **Phoenix 200 MAX** is the best all-round Phoenix dehumidifier. Choose the **Phoenix DryMAX** for portability, the **Phoenix DryMAX XL** for a bit more capacity in a compact body, the **Phoenix 250 MAX** for large open losses and the **Phoenix D385** for cold jobs. If you're a homeowner who wants LGR drying without the fleet price, the **AlorAir Storm LGR Extreme** is the smarter buy — and for a single flood, renting beats both.

faqs.a: Therma-Stor, based in Madison, Wisconsin. The same company makes Santa Fe and Ultra-Aire residential dehumidifiers, while Phoenix is its restoration and professional drying brand.

faqs.q: What is the Phoenix 200 MAX dehumidifier?
faqs.a: A full-size LGR (low grain refrigerant) dehumidifier built for water-damage restoration. It has a built-in condensate pump and is sized for typical jobs like a flooded basement or several wet rooms.

faqs.q: What's the difference between the Phoenix DryMAX and DryMAX XL?
faqs.a: Both are compact LGRs. The XL removes more water in a somewhat larger body, while the standard DryMAX is the easiest to carry and stack. A BLE version of the DryMAX adds Bluetooth monitoring.

faqs.q: Is the Phoenix R250 the same as the 250 MAX?
faqs.a: No. The R250 is an earlier-generation LGR that the 250 MAX replaced. Used R250s can still be good machines if the pump and coil have been maintained, but confirm parts availability with the serial number.

faqs.q: Where can I find a Phoenix DryMAX LGR manual or parts list?
faqs.a: Phoenix posts manuals and technical documents on its website by model. For older units or parts breakdowns, contact a Phoenix distributor with the model and serial number from the data plate.

faqs.q: How much does a Phoenix 200 MAX cost?
faqs.a: Restoration LGRs like the 200 MAX typically cost several thousand dollars new, in the same range as comparable units in our [Dri-Eaz guide](/best/best-dri-eaz-dehumidifier/). Prices vary by dealer and whether accessories are included, so compare restoration suppliers.

They're well regarded in the restoration trade for durability and drying performance. The main drawbacks are cost and weight, which make them a poor value for homeowners with ordinary humidity problems.
